title: Biblical Silences and Modern Questions
description: Explore how ancient scriptures speak to (or are silent on) contemporary issues, inviting us to interpret principles of wisdom, love, and justice for today. A 5-day reflective journey.

dailyReadings.title: Wisdom for New Frontiers
dailyReadings.reflectionPrompt: The Bible doesn't mention AI or genetic engineering. It was written thousands of years before anyone imagined those things. But it does talk about wisdom and seeking understanding. When you're staring at a decision that has no clear 'biblical' answer, how do you find your way?

interspersedInsights.text: Proverbs says if you call out for insight and search for it like hidden treasure, you'll understand the fear of the Lord. Wisdom isn't a formula. It's a pursuit. You don't get it by memorizing a rule book. You get it by wanting it badly enough to go looking. The Bible doesn't answer every question, but it does teach you how to ask better ones.

The Lord gives wisdom. From his mouth come knowledge and understanding. When you hit a question the Bible doesn't directly address, you don't have to panic. You have a source of wisdom bigger than any search engine. The same God who guided people through dilemmas they'd never faced before is still guiding today.

If any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault. That's a promise you can take to the bank. You don't have to have it all figured out before you come to God. You come with your confusion and your uncertainty. And James says God won't roll his eyes at you. He'll give you what you need.

dailyReadings.title: The Spirit of the Law: Love and Inclusion
dailyReadings.reflectionPrompt: Jesus said everything hangs on two commands: love God and love your neighbor. That's the whole thing. When the Bible says things that are hard to reconcile with that, where do you start? Who in your life needs you to lead with love first and figure out the rest as you go?

interspersedInsights.text: Jesus takes the entire Old Testament law and boils it down to love. Love God with everything you've got, and love your neighbor as yourself. Not love your neighbor as long as they look like you or think like you or vote like you. Just love them. If an interpretation of Scripture leads you away from love, you might want to double-check your interpretation.

There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. Paul takes every identity divider his culture had and says they don't hold up anymore. Not in Christ. The walls we build between people, nationality, economic status, gender, they crumble at the foot of the cross. What would it look like if your church actually lived like that was true?

Paul tells the Romans to accept the one whose faith is weak, without quarreling over disputable matters. Who are you to judge someone else's servant? That's a posture of humility. You don't have to have a fully formed opinion on everything. You can hold your convictions and still make room at the table for people who see things differently. The table doesn't belong to you anyway. It belongs to God.

dailyReadings.title: Caring for Our Common Home
dailyReadings.reflectionPrompt: The Bible doesn't use words like 'carbon footprint' or 'climate change.' But it has a lot to say about whose the earth is and how we're supposed to treat it. If the land belongs to God and you're just a tenant, what does that mean for how you live on it?

interspersedInsights.text: God put the man in the garden to work it and take care of it. Before anything went wrong in the world, humans had a job. And the job description was tending the earth. Not exploiting it. Not using it up. Taking care of it. That's the original human vocation. Everything else. Your career, your hobbies, your retirement plan. It all fits inside that bigger calling.

The earth is the Lord's and everything in it. You don't own the ground under your house. You don't own the air in your lungs. God does. That doesn't mean you can't enjoy it. It means you enjoy it like a guest at someone else's table. With gratitude, not entitlement. With care, not carelessness.

The land must not be sold permanently, because the land is mine and you reside in my land as foreigners and strangers. God tells Israel they don't own the land. They're guests. And he commands them to make sure the land can be redeemed, restored, returned. There's a built-in check against permanently exploiting resources. The earth isn't a possession. It's a trust.

dailyReadings.title: Navigating Conflict: Diverse Voices on Peace
dailyReadings.reflectionPrompt: The Bible has 'an eye for an eye' and 'turn the other cheek' in the same book. Not because it's confused, but because it's honest about the tension. When you're hurt by someone, which voice are you more drawn to? The one that wants things to be fair, or the one that wants things to be made new?

interspersedInsights.text: An eye for an eye sounds harsh to modern ears, but in its original context it was actually about limiting revenge. You could only take an eye, not a life. It put a fence around retaliation. But even with that fence, it still keeps the cycle of hurt spinning. It's justice, but it's not healing.

Then Jesus comes along and says turn the other cheek, go the extra mile, give them your cloak too. He's not telling you to be a doormat. He's telling you to break the cycle. When someone slaps you and you turn the other cheek, you're not submitting. You're refusing to play the game. You're saying 'I won't become you.' That's not weakness. That's the hardest kind of strength there is.

Isaiah dreams of a day when nations beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Weapons become farm tools. Things that destroyed become things that grow food. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war anymore. That's the direction God is moving history. Every peacemaker is pulling in that direction.

dailyReadings.title: Faith and Governance
dailyReadings.reflectionPrompt: The Bible tells you to submit to authorities and also to obey God rather than humans. That's a tension, not a contradiction. Where in your own life have you had to weigh loyalty to the system against loyalty to your conscience?

interspersedInsights.text: Israel wanted a king so they could be like all the other nations. Samuel warned them: a king will take your sons for his army, your daughters for his kitchen, your fields for his friends. Power concentrates. It always does. And the people insisted anyway. Sometimes the thing you think you want is the very thing that will undo you. It's worth asking whether the systems you're cheering for will actually serve the people you say you care about.

Paul says to submit to governing authorities because there is no authority except from God. That's a hard teaching, especially if you live under a corrupt or oppressive government. But it's also a reminder that human power is temporary and derivative. No leader sits in office without God's permission. That doesn't mean God approves of everything they do. It means even their authority is on loan.

Peter and the apostles said, 'We must obey God rather than human beings.' They said it right after they'd been told by the authorities to stop talking about Jesus. There's a line. When human authority tells you to do something that contradicts God's heart for justice and love, you follow the higher authority. Knowing where that line is takes wisdom, prayer, and a community of people who'll be honest with you.
